items.title: Corporate Stances on Societal Issues in the US
items.desc: Uses large language models to read 52,000 news articles and press releases on 836 S&P 500 firms, identifying 9,917 corporate stances on partisan issues; stance-taking rose fourfold after 2008, is mostly liberal, and tracks media attention more than lobbying. [arXiv econ.GN, submitted 2026-11-14]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Welcome to a quick explainer, based on the abstract only. The paper is called Corporate Stances on Societal Issues in the US.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The question is when and why companies take public positions on divisive issues like climate change or abortion.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: And the interesting part is how they measured it, right?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Yes. The authors used large language models to read about fifty-two thousand news articles and press releases covering eight hundred thirty-six companies that were in the S&P 500 at some point between 2008 and 2025.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: What did they find?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: They identified nearly ten thousand stances on nine partisan issues. Stance-taking rose fourfold after 2008 and peaked in 2021. It is overwhelmingly liberal and concentrated among the largest firms, and a quarter of stances give no explicit business justification.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Is it lobbying by another name?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Apparently not. Stance-taking is only weakly related to lobbying and campaign contributions, and it does not follow the electoral cycle. Firms tend to speak when media coverage and public interest in an issue peak.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: And who decides what the company says?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Leadership matters. Within a firm, more Democrats among leaders increases liberal stances, and more women increases stances on gender issues and abortion.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: So the takeaway is that corporate speech looks like a contribution to public debate rather than a strategy to shape policy that affects the core business. Remember, this is from the abstract only.

items.title: Are Revealed Preferences All You Need for AI Alignment?
items.desc: A theory paper giving a criterion for when a principal's observed decisions are enough for an AI agent to act on the principal's behalf; they suffice for acting, but for choosing costless evidence they may not, and greater capability can turn that error into wrong actions. [arXiv econ.TH, submitted 2026-11-14]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Quick explainer, based on the abstract only. The paper asks: are revealed preferences all you need for AI alignment?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The setup is that AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: So when is watching choices enough?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The authors give a criterion that holds at every belief the AI might have. For acting, decisions are enough.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: But not for everything.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Right. Cautious actions, like deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks. For choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: And if that fails?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Then the AI acts as its principal would, yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: What fills the gap?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Choices between two mistakes reveal what ordinary decisions miss. That is the takeaway, from the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Why does this matter beyond theory?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Because as AI agents get more capable and act for people in markets and firms, knowing when observed choices fully capture what a person wants tells designers when they need to collect additional signals, such as how people trade off two different mistakes.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: So the lesson is that learning from behavior is powerful for acting but can quietly mislead when the AI must decide what to learn next.

items.title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
items.desc: Models how evolutionary selection shapes an AI agent's tradeoff between task completion and rules of conduct; a learned policy converges to the tradeoffs its environment rewards, and accumulated experience makes this harder to reverse, with small neural-network experiments as illustration. [arXiv cs.AI, submitted 2026-11-13]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Quick explainer, based on the abstract only. The paper is Alignment by Socialization.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: AI agents must finish tasks while following rules of conduct, and those goals can conflict.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: How do the authors study that?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: With a model where copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only copies taking the rewarded action reproduce. Long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: They compare three policies, I think.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Yes. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox that rewards completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as stakes rise. A learned policy converges to the tradeoffs the environment rewards. When humans supply the rewards, they call this socialization.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Does it stick?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Accumulated experience makes it harder to reverse under later task-only training, though violations can occur before the disposition changes, and finite memory weakens protection.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: And hard rules?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: A hard prohibition can prevent a fatal violation, but a mistaken prohibition can be costly. The takeaway: alignment depends on the environments that shape agents, not only on assigned objectives.

sections.name: 📦 Operations & Supply Chain (INFORMS: Management Science, M&SOM, Operations Research)

items.title: OM Forum—Viewing Knowledge Creation as a Supply Chain – Scholarly Purpose in the Age of AI
items.desc: A forum essay treating scholarly knowledge creation as a supply chain of complementary contributions, with a discussion of how AI shifts research bottlenecks and complementarities; it draws four lessons for operations researchers and doctoral training. [M&SOM, published online 2026-11-19]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Quick explainer, based on the abstract only. This is an OM Forum essay in Manufacturing and Service Operations Management.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: It asks where operations scholars should contribute, and what analytical expertise is worth as AI advances.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: What is the core idea?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: View knowledge creation as a supply chain of complementary contributions, shifting attention from a single paper's reach to the capabilities and connections that sustain collective progress.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Four lessons?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Specialization can serve a collective purpose; usable connections are part of a contribution; feedback and inquiry renew capabilities; and faster individual tasks do not necessarily improve the whole process.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Where does AI come in?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The discussion emphasizes research questions and parsimonious modeling, and uses coding and numerical experiments to explain shifting bottlenecks and complementarities.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Takeaway: researchers can ask what their work enables, and choose collaborators who supply missing capabilities.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: What about doctoral training?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The abstract suggests combining methodological depth with practice in evaluating and connecting contributions, and it says editors can assess work within its stated scope while supporting renewal and reuse.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: It also says projects do not each need to span the full process or promise a big immediate impact. Examples include inventory management and process flexibility, and also medical research, soccer and photography.

items.title: Dual Active Learning for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
items.desc: Proposes an algorithm that jointly selects which conversations and which human teachers to query when learning a reward function for aligning LLMs, then applies pessimistic RL; proves a sub-optimality rate of O(1/sqrt(T)) and shows gains in simulations and LLM experiments. [Operations Research, published online 2026-11-20]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Quick explainer, based on the abstract only. The paper is Dual Active Learning for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, in Operations Research.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Aligning large language models with human preferences usually uses human feedback, which is costly and slow.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: So the problem is spending that feedback wisely.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Exactly. Teachers differ in expertise, so the authors design a dual active reward learning algorithm that chooses both which conversations to label and which teacher to ask, motivated by D-optimal design.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Then what?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: They apply pessimistic reinforcement learning on the learned reward estimator. Theoretically, the estimator achieves minimal generalized variance asymptotically, and the policy's sub-optimality scales as one over the square root of the sample budget.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Does it work in practice?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Simulations and experiments on LLMs show it beats state-of-the-art methods, according to the abstract.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Why does it matter for operations?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Labeling is a scarce resource, like any capacity in operations. Choosing which items and which experts to spend it on is a classic experimental design and allocation problem, now applied to making language models behave as people prefer.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Caveat: this is from the abstract only, so details of the experiments are not covered here.
